claims.text: Atomic-size mismatches among constituent metals induce local lattice strain in equimolar multi-metal nanoparticles.
Local lattice strain is the dominant factor governing retention of a single-phase solid solution at high temperature.
Nanoparticles engineered to minimize lattice strain will retain homogeneous structure and chemical distribution throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with enhanced lattice strain will undergo phase segregation or ordering at lower temperatures than low-strain nanoparticles.
Replacing constituent metals with elements of similar atomic radius will reduce local lattice strain.
Replacing constituent metals with elements having more dissimilar atomic radii will increase local lattice strain.
Maintaining the same number of components and equal or near-equal ratios during substitution keeps overall configurational entropy constant.
Lower local lattice strain enhances kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion and clustering.
Higher local lattice strain lowers kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion and clustering.
Increased lattice strain increases atomic mobility under high-temperature conditions.
Increased lattice strain raises the driving force for chemical ordering or phase segregation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution when local strain is low.
Low-strain nanoparticles will show no secondary phases or elemental clustering across 473–1923 K.
High-strain nanoparticles will show secondary phases, ordering, or local elemental clustering at an earlier temperature than the low-strain control.
Five-or-more-metal nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size differences have been shown to retain stable single-phase structures across 473–1923 K.
Particle size, processing conditions, and surface effects can independently stabilize or destabilize the nanoparticles.

Failure of the high-strain samples to segregate, order, or become chemically inhomogeneous earlier or more strongly than the low-strain controls would falsify the proposed dominance of lattice strain.
